evaluation.positioning_hook: A hyper-achieving college sophomore starts slipping through time on a haunted campus and must face her mother’s trauma before a professor with his own dead son pulls her deeper into the loop.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible as elevated genre with a strong emotional engine: a gifted young woman, a haunted campus, and a trauma-driven time-slip mystery. It has clear appeal for streamer audiences and genre buyers, though the intellectual framing and psychological specificity make it more targeted than four-quadrant.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early: Jessica sees a black void on campus, gets pulled into a time-dislocation mystery, and discovers Professor Maddox and Henry are tied to the same phenomenon. The script keeps the rules mysterious, but the central question is clean and easy to pitch.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jessica is a strong lead because she’s overachieving, funny, brittle, and emotionally blocked, which gives the role real play. Maddox and Henry are vivid counterweights, but the script is still most durable through Jessica’s interiority rather than a broad ensemble of equally rich players.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The campus setting, trauma-as-portal idea, and the way the monster reads as a manifestation of dysregulation give the script a distinct angle. The Penderecki sequence, the Discord mythology, and the temporal overlap imagery show a writer making specific, confident choices.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The episode keeps escalating through the campus mystery, the steam tunnels, the time-slip, and the final confrontation with Maddox. It does spend time on atmosphere and psychological framing, but the set pieces are strong enough to keep the engine moving.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s best idea is that the supernatural threat and the protagonist’s trauma are not separate systems but the same one. That makes the time-travel conceit feel emotionally inevitable rather than decorative, especially in the mother/son parallel between Jessica and Henry.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Morgan College feels specific and story-generating: elite liberal-arts status, dorm folklore, Discord gossip, steam tunnels, old frat-house architecture, and campus social hierarchy all feed the plot. The world has enough institutional texture to support the mystery without feeling generic.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually calibrated: collegiate, eerie, funny, and psychologically raw all at once. The script can pivot from drunken banter to body-horror-adjacent dread to emotional confession without losing its identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The Maddox/Henry/Jessica triangle suggests a much larger emotional and temporal architecture beneath the surface. The script withholds enough to imply a deeper mythology while still giving the audience a satisfying first-episode turn.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jessica/Kerri gives the script a reliable emotional anchor, and Maddox/Henry/Donovan create a useful triangle of pressure and suspicion. It’s not an ensemble machine in the broad sense, but the recurring relationships are strong enough to generate repeated story energy.

lead_characters.name: Jessica Wolfe
lead_characters.demographics: female, 19, college sophomore, high-achieving, upper-middle-class or affluent academic striver
lead_characters.hook: Jessica is a hyper-competent, overbooked honors student who performs control so well she can even be the funniest drunk in the room. Underneath the polish is a daughter still carrying her mother’s illness and death, and the script makes her emotional repression the literal engine of the supernatural plot.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is showcase territory in the vein of Florence Pugh in Midsommar or Emma Stone in The Curse — a role that lets an actor play intelligence, panic, denial, and emotional collapse in the same frame. It’s a prestige lead with genre propulsion and a big internal transformation.

lead_characters.name: Kerri
lead_characters.demographics: female, 19, college sophomore, close friend, athlete/performer
lead_characters.hook: Kerri is Jessica’s blunt, affectionate best friend — the one person who can puncture her self-seriousness without losing the friendship. She’s socially fluent, skeptical, and loyal, which makes her the script’s emotional reality check whenever Jessica starts to drift into the uncanny.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp best-friend role that gives an actor the fast, scene-stealing rhythm of Beanie Feldstein in Booksmart or Ayo Edebiri in supporting-comedy mode. The appeal is the comic authority plus the ability to turn into a grounded emotional anchor.

lead_characters.name: Donovan
lead_characters.demographics: male, 20, college junior, awkward, socially isolated, bearded
lead_characters.hook: Donovan is the campus outsider who turns obsession into performance art and conspiracy lore. He’s needy, earnest, and a little creepy, but the script gives him enough sincerity that he reads as a damaged believer rather than a stock incel punchline.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor material in the mold of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or Justice Smith in a more anxious register — a role that lets an actor play awkwardness, longing, and volatility without ever becoming generic.

lead_characters.name: William Maddox
lead_characters.demographics: male, early 60s, professor, widowed or bereaved father, intellectually formidable
lead_characters.hook: Maddox is a brilliant, handsome professor who weaponizes empathy as a method and grief as a theory. He’s part mentor, part manipulator, part gatekeeper, and the script keeps him just slippery enough that every scene with him feels like a test Jessica may already be failing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of prestige supporting role that gives an actor the delicious ambiguity of Michael Stuhlbarg in Call Me by Your Name or Matthew Rhys in a darker mode — authority, seduction, menace, and grief all in one performance.

lead_characters.name: Henry Maddox
lead_characters.demographics: male, 19, college student, mentally unstable, charismatic, drugged, deceased in present timeline
lead_characters.hook: Henry is the dead son at the center of the campus mythology, but the script makes him feel alive through his wit, instability, and romantic self-mythologizing. He’s seductive, wounded, and dangerous, with enough charm to make Jessica believe he might be the key to everything.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can break out for a young actor the way Lucas Hedges or Timothée Chalamet early roles did — emotionally volatile, intellectually alive, and carrying a tragic charge that lingers after the scene ends.

lead_characters.name: Jessica's Mother
lead_characters.demographics: female, 20s-30s in flashbacks, young mother, mentally ill
lead_characters.hook: Jessica’s mother appears as both memory and wound: loving, erratic, frightening, and impossible to fully hold onto. She’s not just backstory; she’s the emotional source code for Jessica’s fear, guilt, and need to control reality.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of flashback role that can become a devastating showcase in the mold of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April — brief screen time with major emotional aftershock.

lead_characters.name: Jessica's Father
lead_characters.demographics: male, middle-aged, doctor or clinician, supportive parent
lead_characters.hook: Jessica’s father is the calm voice of ordinary life, the one person who still treats her like a daughter instead of a problem to solve. He’s not flashy, but he gives the script a crucial baseline of care and normalcy that makes Jessica’s dislocation hit harder.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a grounded, emotionally precise supporting role in the vein of Richard Jenkins in The Visitor or Kyle Chandler in a family-drama register — a quiet performance that can land hard with very little screen time.

casting_characteristics: flashback mother role requires younger adult casting

notable_requirements: elite New England college campus look
library, dorm, classroom, office, parking lot, pond/bird sanctuary

technical.vfx_details: Temporal overlap, disappearing buildings, two-moon sky, black void monster, and reality-shift transitions require compositing and selective digital enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical lighting shifts, phone-signal effects, environmental distortion, and a suicide-video insert; no large-scale effects package.

rights_flags.detail: Krzysztof Penderecki's 'Threnody for the Victims of Hiroshima' is specifically named and used as a plot/characterization beat.
The pop song the women sing drunkenly is referenced as a specific source cue and may require clearance if retained as named or used on soundtrack.
The Matrix is specifically named in dialogue.
Twilight is specifically named in dialogue and flashback context.
Discord is central to the campus mythology and online chatter.
YouTube is used as a specific platform reference in the self-dysregulation montage.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: elevated genre theatrical or streamer-first with festival launch potential.

budget.note: The campus footprint is manageable, but the time-slip visuals, reality-overlap moments, and black-void monster will need disciplined VFX scope to stay inside an indie-to-mid budget.

casting.note: Jessica has to carry comedy, panic, intellect, and emotional breakdown; Maddox needs authority plus ambiguity; Henry needs charisma without losing instability. Those are all castable, but the lead and professor roles are the real lift.

development.note: The script’s mythology is compelling, but the buyer conversation will focus on how much of the time-travel system is legible versus intentionally withheld in a feature runtime.

comp_set.title: The Blackcoat's Daughter
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the eerie, female-led, psychologically haunted genre lane where trauma and supernatural dread are fused into one atmosphere.

comp_set.title: Coherence
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it uses a contained social setting and reality slippage to turn a small cast into a high-concept puzzle.

comp_set.title: The Invitation
comp_set.why_it_comps: The slow-burn suspicion, social unease, and eventual reality rupture are structurally similar, even though the setting is campus rather than dinner-party.

comp_set.title: I Saw the TV Glow
comp_set.why_it_comps: The emotional logic of identity, dissociation, and uncanny media/trauma overlap is very close to this script’s psychological register.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated horror and prestige sci-fi with an emotional wound at the center, especially viewers drawn to campus settings and psychologically unstable mysteries.
audience_target.demographics: 18-44 skew, slightly female-leaning, college-educated, streamer-native, genre-literate audience

budget_tier.note: Contemporary campus locations, a small speaking cast, and selective VFX keep this in indie territory, with the monster/time-shift effects as the main scope driver.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where psychological horror, identity drama, and a clean high-concept hook can be sold on taste and execution rather than spectacle. The college setting and emotional specificity make it especially attractive to buyers looking for smart genre with awards-adjacent credibility.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the mythology is expandable, but no side character or world element on the page is yet strong enough to justify a sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.what_it_means: That gives the film a clean commercial identity: the horror is not decorative, it is emotionally legible and marketable as prestige genre. Buyers chasing elevated horror and actors looking for psychologically loaded material will both understand the promise immediately.
strengths.evidence: Jessica’s panic around her mother’s illness is repeatedly mirrored by the black void, and Maddox explicitly frames the monster as trauma externalized.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jessica is a real lead role
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives a buyer a female protagonist with range — funny, brilliant, ashamed, frightened, and finally destabilized — which is exactly the kind of part that can attract a name actress. That makes the project easier to package than a concept-only genre piece.
strengths.evidence: Her drunken Martin Eden riff, her confrontation with Maddox, and her breakdown in the steam tunnels all show different performance registers.

strengths.what_it_means: Morgan College feels specific enough to function as a story engine, which helps the film stand out in a crowded genre market. Buyers get a contained but not generic setting with built-in social hierarchy, folklore, and institutional secrecy.
strengths.evidence: The Discord threads, steam tunnels, old frat house, admissions-board professor, and elite liberal-arts branding all feed the plot.

strengths.what_it_means: The script keeps adding information without losing the central question, which is a strong sign for audience retention and word-of-mouth. That kind of controlled escalation is valuable to streamers and genre distributors alike.
strengths.evidence: The black void, Maddox’s journal, the steam tunnels, the time-slip, and the final reveal of Jessica’s mother all land as successive turns.

strengths.what_it_means: The Jessica/Maddox/Henry triangle creates roles that can attract serious actors who want material with psychological stakes, not just plot mechanics. That broadens the buyer conversation beyond horror specialists.
strengths.evidence: Maddox’s manipulative tenderness, Henry’s unstable charisma, and Jessica’s emotional resistance all read as actor-forward writing.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, actor-friendly elevated genre feature with a clean hook: a high-achieving college sophomore discovers her trauma is literally warping time and reality. The contained campus footprint, strong lead role, and prestige-horror tone make it a credible buy for streamer originals or boutique genre financiers looking for something smarter than a standard scare piece.

items.detail: The script is strongest when it’s emotional and uncanny, but the rules of the time-slip, the monster, and Maddox’s knowledge are still more suggestive than concrete. That’s fine for a first installment, but buyers will immediately weigh how much clarity they need before committing to a feature-length version.

items.area: Jessica’s internal wound drives the whole engine.
items.detail: Nearly every major turn depends on Jessica’s trauma response, which is a strength creatively but also a concentration risk commercially. If the lead performance doesn’t land, the entire movie’s emotional and narrative architecture gets narrower fast.

items.area: The VFX ask is modest but real.
items.detail: The black void monster, the two-reality sky, the disappearing building, and the time-shift transitions all need to look intentional rather than improvised. That keeps this out of true microbudget territory and makes visual discipline a real greenlight conversation.

items.area: Named music and pop-culture references need a pass.
items.detail: Penderecki’s 'Threnody for the Victims of Hiroshima,' The Matrix, Twilight, Discord, and YouTube are all specifically named. None of that is fatal, but the script is not clearance-neutral, and the music cue in particular is a real budget/legal line item.

issues.headline: The main friction is that the script’s power comes from a deliberately unstable mythology and a lead performance that has to carry the emotional logic of the whole piece. Add a real but manageable VFX burden plus a handful of named-music/IP references, and this becomes a smart buy only if the package is disciplined.
